parsed.answer: Intel's operating margin for fiscal 2024 (full year) was -22.0%. That is an operating loss of $11,678 million on revenue of $53,101 million (operating income ÷ revenue).

Microsoft's operating margin rose by about 4.0 percentage points between fiscal 2021 and fiscal 2025, from 41.6% to 45.6%. Microsoft's fiscal year ends June 30.

- FY2021 (ended June 30, 2021): operating income $69,916 million on revenue of $168,088 million, an operating margin of 41.6%.
- FY2025 (ended June 30, 2025): operating income $128,528 million on revenue of $281,724 million, an operating margin of 45.6%.

Operating margin is operating income divided by revenue. I calculated the change as 45.62% − 41.59% ≈ 4.0 percentage points.

Operating income grew faster than revenue over the period (about 84% versus about 68%), which is what lifted the margin. I did not search the filings for the reasons behind this.

parsed.answer:
In fiscal 2023, Intel spent the largest share of revenue on R&D at 29.6%. NVIDIA was next at 27.2%, and AMD was lowest at 25.9%.

- Intel: R&D $16,046M on revenue $54,228M, which is 29.6%.
- NVIDIA: R&D $7,339M on revenue $26,974M, which is 27.2%.
- AMD: R&D $5,872M on revenue $22,680M, which is 25.9%.

The percentage is R&D expense divided by revenue, taken from the stored metric records.

The fiscal years end at different times. From general background knowledge, not from the database: NVIDIA's fiscal 2023 ended in late January 2023. AMD's and Intel's fiscal 2023 both ended in late December 2023. NVIDIA's period therefore covers roughly the 2022 calendar year, about 11 months earlier than the other two.

Intel spent the most in absolute terms, at roughly 2 to 3 times the R&D of the other two. That reflects its much larger revenue base.

NVIDIA's R&D spending as a share of revenue fell from 19.6% in fiscal 2022 to 9.9% in fiscal 2025. It was not a steady decline, because the ratio rose in fiscal 2023 and then dropped sharply.

- FY2022: 19.6% (R&D $5,268 million on revenue of $26,914 million)
- FY2023: 27.2% (R&D $7,339 million on revenue of $26,974 million)
- FY2024: 14.2% (R&D $8,675 million on revenue of $60,922 million)
- FY2025: 9.9% (R&D $12,914 million on revenue of $130,497 million)

Over the whole period the ratio fell by about 9.7 percentage points (19.6% minus 9.9%, computed from the unrounded ratios).

The ratio rose in FY2023 because revenue was almost flat (about $26.9 billion to $27.0 billion) while R&D grew. It then fell in FY2024 and FY2025 because revenue grew much faster than R&D. Revenue rose about 4.8 times from FY2022 to FY2025, while R&D rose about 2.5 times. The dollar amount of R&D increased every year.

The fiscal-year-end dates come from general background knowledge, not from the database. NVIDIA's fiscal year ends in late January, so FY2022 ended in January 2022 and FY2025 ended in January 2025.

AMD's management attributed the drop in operating income in fiscal 2022 (year ended December 31, 2022) primarily to amortization of intangible assets from the Xilinx acquisition. The MD&A says: "Operating income for 2022 was $1.3 billion compared to operating income of $3.6 billion for 2021. The decrease in operating income was primarily driven by amortization of intangible assets associated with the Xilinx acquisition."

Supporting detail from the MD&A: in 2022, cost of sales and operating expense included $1.4 billion and $2.1 billion of amortization expense, respectively, from intangibles acquired in the Xilinx and Pensando acquisitions. Gross margin also fell to 45% from 48% for the same reason.

Operating income was $1,264 million on revenue of $23,601 million. That gives an operating margin of 5.4% for fiscal 2022. Operating income fell 65.4% from $3,648 million in fiscal 2021 (year ended December 25, 2021).

NVIDIA's gross margin fell from 64.9% in fiscal 2022 (year ended January 30, 2022) to 56.9% in fiscal 2023 (year ended January 29, 2023). That is a decline of 8.0 percentage points. Revenue was almost flat, at $26,974 million against $26,914 million. Gross profit fell from $17,475 million to $15,356 million.

Why: the 10-K says the decrease "was primarily due to $2.17 billion of inventory provisions in fiscal year 2023." The provisions had two parts:
- About $1.04 billion for inventory on hand.
- About $1.13 billion for inventory purchase obligations in excess of NVIDIA's current demand projections.

The filing says the charges largely related to excess supply of NVIDIA Ampere architecture Gaming and Data Center products compared with demand expectations, particularly expected demand in China.

Provisions were $354 million in fiscal 2022. After $137 million of sales of previously written-off inventory (fiscal 2022: $111 million), the net effect on gross margin was an unfavorable 7.5 points in fiscal 2023, against 0.9 points in fiscal 2022. So inventory charges explain most of the 8.0-point decline.

parsed.answer:
**Short answer:** Yes. The reported figures support management's explanation. Intel's 10-K attributes the fall in gross margin to lower sales of PC and server chips, higher unit costs, and higher one-time charges. The figures show a 20% revenue drop while cost of revenue rose.

**What the reported figures show (fiscal 2022 vs. fiscal 2021, years ending in late December)**
- Revenue fell from $79,024M to $63,054M (-20.2%).
- Cost of revenue rose from $35,209M to $36,188M (+2.8%).
- Gross profit fell from $43,815M to $26,866M. That is a $16.9B (-38.7%) drop, which the 10-K calls 39%.
- Gross margin fell from 55.4% to 42.6%, a drop of about 12.8 percentage points (my calculation).

Revenue fell sharply while costs did not fall. Intel has high fixed manufacturing costs, and the risk factors say lower demand can disproportionately hit gross margin.

**What management said drove it.** The MD&A (Item 7) has a gross margin bridge. It lists these items as reductions in gross margin dollars, in millions:
- Lower CCG (client computing) revenue, driven by notebook and desktop: $(4,673)
- Lower DCAI (data center) server revenue: $(3,330)
- Higher unit cost, "primarily from increased mix of Intel 7 products and 10nm SuperFin": $(2,663)
- Higher period charges, "primarily driven by inventory reserves taken in 2022": $(2,159)
- Higher period charges tied to the ramp of Intel 4 and other product enhancements: $(2,012)
- Lower gross margin from the divested NAND memory business: $(1,995)
- Optane inventory impairment: $(723)
- Higher excess capacity charges: $(423)
- Partial offsets: higher gross margin from DCAI other products (+$702) and NEX Ethernet (+$522)

**Do the numbers support it?** Yes. The bridge items add up to the total decline: $26,866M − $43,815M = −$16,949M.
- Lower PC and server volume is the largest driver. CCG and DCAI together are $(8,003)M, about 47% of the decline (my calculation). That matches revenue falling 20% against roughly flat costs.
- Unit cost and period charges explain much of the rest. The inventory, Intel 4 ramp, Optane and excess capacity charges total about $(5,317)M (my calculation). Unit cost adds $(2,663)M. This fits cost of revenue rising 2.8% while revenue fell.
- The NAND divestiture adds $(1,995)M.

**Caveat:** The data do not separate price from volume, so I can't say how much of the CCG and DCAI decline came from lower prices rather than lower units. The bridge also reflects management's own categorization.

The premise is incorrect. Intel's revenue did not grow every year from fiscal 2019 through fiscal 2023. It rose in fiscal 2020 and 2021, then fell in fiscal 2022 and 2023.

Intel's annual revenue (fiscal years end in late December):
- FY2019 (ended Dec 28, 2019): $71,965 million
- FY2020 (ended Dec 26, 2020): $77,867 million, up about 8.2%
- FY2021 (ended Dec 25, 2021): $79,024 million, up about 1.5%
- FY2022 (ended Dec 31, 2022): $63,054 million, down about 20.2%
- FY2023 (ended Dec 30, 2023): $54,228 million, down about 14.0%

Over the whole period, revenue fell by $17,737 million, from $71,965 million to $54,228 million. That is a decline of about 24.6%, so total growth was negative. I calculated these figures from the reported revenue records.

parsed.answer:
Microsoft's operating margin fell by about 0.3 percentage points. It went from 42.1% in fiscal 2022 to 41.8% in fiscal 2023. Both fiscal years end June 30. The unrounded figures are 42.06% and 41.77%, a difference of about 0.28 points (computed).

Operating income still grew, from $83,383 million to $88,523 million. That is an increase of $5.1 billion, or 6%. Revenue grew a little faster, from $198,270 million to $211,915 million, so the margin slipped slightly.

The filing points to these drivers:
- **Q2 charge:** On January 18, 2023, Microsoft announced decisions to align its cost structure with demand and consolidate office space. It recorded a $1.2 billion charge in the second quarter of fiscal 2023. The charge included $800 million of employee severance, impairment charges from changes to the hardware portfolio, and lease consolidation costs. The filing says it reduced operating income by $1.2 billion.
- **Operating expenses:** The filing says they "increased $5.3 billion or 10% driven by employee severance expenses, 2 points of growth from the Nuance and Xandr acquisitions, investments in cloud engineering, and LinkedIn." General and administrative expense rose 28%. The filing attributes that to severance and a charge tied to a non-public preliminary draft decision from the Irish Data Protection Commission.
- **Gross margin:** The gross margin percentage rose slightly. That was helped by a change in accounting estimate. Excluding that change, the gross margin percentage fell 1 point. The filing says this was driven by declines in Intelligent Cloud and More Personal Computing, partly offset by sales mix shift between segments.
- **Segments:** More Personal Computing operating income fell $4.0 billion, or 20%. That offset growth in Productivity and Business Processes and in Intelligent Cloud.

The filing text does not give a single calculation of how much each factor moved the margin. The ranking of drivers above is therefore not quantified.

parsed.answer:
No. The database shows Intel's fiscal 2023 gross margin (year ended December 2023) was 40.0%, not 55%. Gross profit was $21,711 million on revenue of $54,228 million. In fiscal 2022 it was 42.6% ($26,866 million on $63,054 million). That is a decline of about 2.6 percentage points, which I calculated as 42.6% minus 40.0%.

Intel's 10-K MD&A says gross margin dollars fell $5.2 billion, or 19%, from 2022. Revenue fell 14% over the same period. Its year-over-year bridge of gross margin dollars lists these drivers:
- **Lower server product margin:** -$2,709 million, mainly from lower server revenue.
- **Lower NEX product margin:** -$1,832 million, from lower revenue across NEX product lines.
- **Lower notebook and desktop product margin:** -$1,704 million, from lower notebook and desktop revenue.
- **Higher unit cost:** -$1,654 million, mainly from a higher mix of Intel 7 products.
- **Excess capacity charges:** -$411 million, higher period charges.
- **Partial offsets:**
  - +$1,973 million, from lower period charges as previously reserved inventory sold through and fewer reserves were taken in 2023.
  - +$788 million, from lower product ramp costs.
  - +$723 million, from the absence of the 2022 Optane inventory impairment.

Intel also said that lengthening the useful life of certain production equipment from 5 to 8 years, effective January 2023, increased gross margin by roughly $2.5 billion. Intel calls this an estimate and says the actual impact is impractical to quantify precisely.

The filing's text says the CCG and DCAI segments produced most of the gross margin.

Intel's revenue and operating margin both fell every year from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2024, but the margin fell much faster than revenue. The percentage changes below are my own calculations from the reported figures.

- FY2021 (ended Dec 25, 2021): revenue $79,024 million, operating income $19,456 million, operating margin 24.6%.
- FY2022 (ended Dec 31, 2022): revenue $63,054 million (-20.2% vs. FY2021), operating income $2,334 million, operating margin 3.7%.
- FY2023 (ended Dec 30, 2023): revenue $54,228 million (-14.0% vs. FY2022), operating income $93 million, operating margin 0.2%.
- FY2024 (ended Dec 28, 2024): revenue $53,101 million (-2.1% vs. FY2023), operating income -$11,678 million, operating margin -22.0%.

Overall, from FY2021 to FY2024 revenue fell about 32.8%, or $25,923 million. Operating margin fell by about 46.6 percentage points, from 24.6% to -22.0%.

- FY2022 had the steepest revenue drop (-20.2%). Operating income fell by about 88% and the margin dropped by roughly 21 points.
- In FY2023 revenue fell a further 14.0%, and operating income was close to zero at $93 million.
- In FY2024 revenue was nearly flat (-2.1%), yet Intel swung to an operating loss of $11,678 million, so the margin fell by about 22 points.

The margin fell faster than revenue because operating income dropped far more than sales did. That pattern suggests costs did not come down in line with revenue, but I did not check the filing text for the specific causes, so I can't say what drove it.

Operating margin is operating income divided by revenue, as stored in the database.

Intel's fiscal 2024 10-K (filed 2025) describes Intel Foundry as a "systems foundry" for the AI era. It would serve both Intel's own products and external customers. The main points below come from the MD&A and Risk Factors.

**Goal and positioning**
- Intel Foundry, "comprising technology development, manufacturing and foundry services, seeks to deliver the best systems foundry capabilities to support Intel Products and external customers." It cites three advantages: a robust design ecosystem with key industry partners, systems-of-chips capabilities, and a secure, resilient and sustainable supply chain. (MD&A Overview, 0000050863-25-000009:7:0089)
- Intel says it is "aiming to become a major provider of semiconductor manufacturing solutions for third parties." It still expects its factories to "mostly produce our own products for many years to come." (0000050863-25-000009:7:0092)

**Why internal and external volume fit together**
- Intel's own product volume provides the scale that leading-edge foundry operations need. It also helps "derisk" the foundry offering for third-party customers. (0000050863-25-000009:7:0092)
- External customers would add further scale at the leading edge. On mature nodes they would allow "better monetization of our technology and manufacturing facility investments." (0000050863-25-000009:7:0092)

**Structure**
- Intel plans to make Intel Foundry an independent subsidiary. The stated aims are clearer separation and independence for foundry customers and suppliers, and more flexibility to evaluate separate funding and capital structures. (0000050863-25-000009:7:0092)
- Risk Factors say this includes an internal foundry operating model. That model separates the manufacturing side from the product business units, and it requires a new enterprise resource planning system. Intel is also working to run Intel Foundry, Altera and IMS as majority-owned, autonomous subsidiaries. (0000050863-25-000009:1A:0020)

**Offerings and roadmap**
- Intel Foundry aims to deliver leading-edge process technology and to build out mature-node offerings for third parties. It offers a geographically balanced factory network. Intel expects volume production on its 2nm node, Intel 18A, in 2025. (0000050863-25-000009:7:0093)
- Process technologies for external customers are expected to include Intel 18A (RibbonFET and PowerVia), Intel 3 (EUV), Intel 7, Intel 16, and a new 12nm process being developed with UMC. Intel has also announced Intel 14A as an extension of the roadmap beyond 18A. (0000050863-25-000009:7:0095)
- Advanced packaging and the Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) standard are part of the offering. The offering also relies on an ecosystem of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, intellectual property and design services, so customers can design with Intel as they would with other foundries. (0000050863-25-000009:7:0094, 0000050863-25-000009:7:0095)

**Risks the filing flags**
- Intel has "limited experience in the highly competitive and capital-intensive third-party foundry business." It faces established competitors: TSMC, Samsung, GlobalFoundries, UMC and SMIC. (0000050863-25-000009:1A:0007)
- Implementing the foundry strategy requires significant internal structural, systems and process changes, and the filing notes that significant business changes are "inherently risky." (0000050863-25-000009:1A:0020)

Both answers come from the fiscal 2025 10-Ks, which are the most recent for each company in the database. I did not check the exact fiscal year-end dates in the tools. Each company names the other as its main x86 rival, and each frames its own position a little differently.

**AMD's 10-K**
- Client and Gaming: "Our primary competitor in the supply of CPUs and APUs is Intel." AMD also notes that Arm-based PC platforms "could lead to further adoption of Arm-based PC solutions." (paragraph 0000002488-26-000018:1:0077)
- Data Center: "we compete primarily against Intel Corporation (Intel) and Nvidia Corporation (Nvidia with our CPU, GPU DPU and AI NIC server products." Some customers are also building their own data center chips. (0000002488-26-000018:1:0076)
- Graphics: AMD names Nvidia, the discrete GPU market share leader, as its principal discrete graphics competitor. It also names Intel, "who manufactures and sells integrated graphics processors and gaming-focused discrete GPUs." AMD says it is "the market share leader in semi-custom game console products." (0000002488-26-000018:1:0079)
- Embedded: "Intel is our main competitor for embedded CPUs." (0000002488-26-000018:1:0080)
- Risk factors: AMD does not single out Intel here. It says "Some of our competitors may possess stronger market positions, larger customer bases, more design wins, and greater financial, sales, marketing, and distribution resources than us." It also flags the growth of the Arm ecosystem. (0000002488-26-000018:1A:0049)

**Intel's 10-K**
- Client (CCG): "CCG's primary competitor is AMD, which like us designs processors based on the x86 architecture." Intel says it also faces significant competition from Arm-based designs from Apple, Qualcomm and MediaTek. It adds that it expects the competitive environment to intensify further. (0000050863-26-000011:1:0032)
- Data center and AI (DCAI): AMD "competes with us across the full spectrum of CPUs, GPUs, accelerators and other products." Intel says NVIDIA's GPU systems "have experienced the highest demand in the market." It also lists hyperscalers' custom silicon and Arm- and RISC-V-based products as competitors. (0000050863-26-000011:1:0036)
- Risk factors: Intel lists AMD and Qualcomm as platform competitors, and NVIDIA and AMD as GPU competitors. It stresses Arm's growing ecosystem, and it cites Apple's move to its own Arm-based chips and hyperscalers' in-house designs. (0000050863-26-000011:1A:0004)

**Comparison**
- Both companies call the other the primary x86 competitor in PC and client processors.
- Neither 10-K makes a claim about market share or relative strength against the other. Each describes the rivalry as one of several fronts.
- AMD treats Intel as one competitor alongside Nvidia and Arm, and says some rivals have greater resources.
- Intel puts as much weight on Arm-based rivals, NVIDIA and customers' custom chips as on AMD.

It says the Notified Advanced Computing (NAC) process "has not resulted in approvals for exports of products to customers in China." It also says licenses for D1 and D4 countries carried "onerous" conditions (0001045810-25-000023:1A:0178).
- **Operational changes.** NVIDIA moved some testing, validation, and supply and distribution operations out of China and Hong Kong after the 2022 controls. It warns that any future moves could be costly (0001045810-25-000023:1A:0178).
- **Downstream effects.** Controls have subjected downstream users to restrictions on use, resale, repair or transfer of its products (0001045810-25-000023:1A:0162).
- **Competitive harm.** The FY2023 filing said the rules "may" disadvantage NVIDIA. FY2025 says the existing controls "already have disadvantaged" it and that "Our competitive position has been harmed by the existing export controls" (0001045810-25-000023:1A:0178 and 0001045810-25-000023:1A:0179).
- **China's response.** The FY2025 filing adds Chinese government actions, including an Action Plan on data-center accelerator performance standards (0001045810-25-000023:1A:0182). The FY2023 filing mentioned only Chinese limits on gaming and oversight of digital platform companies (0001045810-23-000017:1A:0157).

**Summary:** The risk grew from one rule aimed at China and Russia, with an A800 workaround, into controls covering many countries and product lines. parsed.answer: In its most recent 10-K (fiscal year 2025), AMD reports three segments: (1) Data Center, which primarily includes AI accelerators, CPUs for servers, GPUs, APUs, DPUs, AI NICs, FPGAs and SoC products for data centers. (2) Client and Gaming, which primarily includes CPUs, APUs, chipsets for desktops and notebooks, discrete GPUs, and semi-custom SoC products and development services. (3) Embedded, which primarily includes embedded CPUs, APUs, FPGAs, SOMs, and adaptive SoC products. Beginning in Q1 of fiscal 2025, AMD combined the former Client and Gaming segments into one reportable segment, and prior-period segment data were retrospectively adjusted. Before that change (for example in the FY2022 10-K), the segments were reported separately, so older filings show four segments: Data Center, Client, Gaming and Embedded. That earlier four-segment count comes from my reading of the FY2022 overview and the combination note, not from a quoted list.

- Q2 FY2027: gross margin was 75.0%. That is gross profit of $72,142 million divided by revenue of $96,221 million.

The change is 74.975% minus 74.934%, which is about +0.04 percentage points. Gross profit grew by about $11.0 billion and revenue by about $14.6 billion, so the two grew at nearly the same rate. I did not look up the drivers of the margin in the filing text.
